nameStory: These little armored critters earned the name 'woodlouse' because they're commonly found hiding under rotting logs and wooden boards, even though they're not actually insects at all! The 'rough' part of their name comes from their bumpy, textured back that feels gritty when you gently touch one. Despite their name suggesting they harm wood, they're actually helpful decomposers that clean up dead plant material.
description: Common rough woodlice are small, oval-shaped creatures that look like tiny armadillos, measuring about half an inch long. They have segmented, gray to brownish bodies covered in bumpy plates that give them their characteristic rough texture. These land-dwelling crustaceans are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects! When disturbed, they can partially roll up into a ball, though not as completely as their pill bug cousins.

idTips.label: Rough, bumpy texture
idTips.description: The back feels distinctly gritty and rough when gently touched, like fine sandpaper, unlike the smoother pill bugs

idTips.label: Partial rolling ability
idTips.description: Can curl up somewhat when threatened but cannot form a complete, tight ball like pill bugs do

idTips.label: Seven pairs of legs
idTips.description: Count the walking legs visible along the sides - always seven pairs on these oval, segmented bodies

idTips.label: Gray to brown coloration
idTips.description: Usually mottled gray, brown, or sometimes yellowish, often with lighter spots or patches

idTips.label: Two pairs of antennae
idTips.description: Look closely at the head for one long pair of antennae and one very short pair that's barely visible

habitat: Look for common rough woodlice in damp, dark places throughout New England - under logs, rocks, leaf litter, and mulch in gardens and forests. They thrive in moist environments like basements, compost piles, and anywhere organic matter is decomposing. You'll often find large groups huddled together under the same log or stone.

seasonality.spring: Active and easy to spot as they emerge from winter hiding spots under logs and stones. Look for them in garden mulch and compost areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid weather and after rain. Often found in large groups under boards, potted plants, and in damp basement areas.
seasonality.fall: Busy feeding on fallen leaves and seeking shelter under deeper layers of mulch and debris as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, stones, and in protected areas, though occasionally visible on warmer days in heated buildings.

funFact: These little land-dwellers actually breathe through gills just like their ocean-dwelling lobster relatives, which is why they must stay moist to survive - they can literally drown in water but also suffocate if they dry out!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with pill bugs (roly-polies), but rough woodlice can't roll into a complete ball and have that distinctive sandpaper-rough texture. Memory trick: 'Rough woodlice can't roll right' - if it makes a perfect ball, it's a pill bug!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'woodlice,' these creatures aren't lice at all and don't harm wood - they're actually beneficial crustaceans that help break down dead organic matter. The name confusion has led many people to think they're pests, when they're actually nature's cleanup crew.
compareHints: The main relative in New England is the brickwork woodlouse, but rough woodlice are much more common and widespread. Brickwork woodlice tend to be found more often around human structures and have a slightly different body shape. The rough, gritty texture remains the most reliable way to identify this particular species among the woodlouse family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Brickwork Woodlouse differs from its close relative, the Common Rough Woodlouse, primarily in its distinctive pale brick-like pattern and the prominent spiny projections on its front corners.
